title: Beating Time
bodyMd:
**Humanities.** This passage is adapted from an original essay on tempo in Western classical music. All persons and incidents in it are invented.

Before the clockwork metronome, a composer who wanted a piece played quickly wrote *allegro* and trusted the performer. The word carried no number. It meant cheerful as much as fast, and how fast depended on the room, the instrument and the period in which the music was played. Then a mechanic named Ferrand patented a pendulum with a sliding weight, and for the first time a composer could write *120* and mean 120.

The invention was greeted as a rescue. One symphonist, who had complained for years that his markings were ignored, went back through his published scores and supplied numbers for many of them. Musicians have been arguing about those numbers ever since. A good many are, by the standards of modern performance, impossibly fast. The explanations offered are ingenious and mutually exclusive: the machine was faulty; the composer misread its scale; illness had distorted his sense of pace; or — the least comfortable possibility — he meant exactly what he wrote, and two centuries of performers have simply grown slower.

What the argument reveals is not a fact about one composer but a limit of notation. A metronome mark fixes a rate; it does not fix a tempo. Tempo, as players use the word, includes the weight of a downbeat, the air left around a phrase, the slight broadening that lets a cadence land. None of that is a number, and a number cannot forbid it. The mark tells the performer where to begin negotiating, not where to stop.

There is a quieter consequence. Once a tempo could be specified, it could also be enforced, and the device moved from the composer's desk to the practice room, where it became less a measure than a judge. Students who learn to play with it often describe the same difficulty: the machine keeps perfect time, and perfect time is not the same as good time.
accessibilityText: A four-paragraph humanities essay about tempo markings in Western classical music. The first paragraph explains that before the clockwork metronome a composer wrote an Italian word such as allegro, which carried no number, and that speed depended on the room, the instrument and the period, until a mechanic named Ferrand patented a pendulum with a sliding weight. The second paragraph describes a symphonist who added numbers to his published scores, notes that many of those numbers seem impossibly fast today, and lists four mutually exclusive explanations: a faulty machine, a misread scale, illness distorting his sense of pace, or the possibility that he meant what he wrote and later performers have grown slower. The third paragraph argues that the dispute reveals a limit of notation, because a metronome mark fixes a rate but not the weight of a downbeat, the air around a phrase or the broadening at a cadence. The fourth paragraph observes that once tempo could be specified it could be enforced, so the device moved to the practice room and became less a measure than a judge, and that perfect time is not the same as good time. The composer, the mechanic Ferrand and all incidents are invented.

provenance.notes: Original humanities passage written for this bank. The mechanic Ferrand, the unnamed symphonist and every detail of the dispute are invented; the passage deliberately avoids naming any real inventor, composer or work. Nothing here is drawn from, or modelled on, any ACT-published Reading passage or any real published essay.
